biography.background: Born October 11, 1967; raised upstate New York; moved to Atlanta 1998. Former marketing/media executive turned state legislator. Husband Daniel; three children. Has lived in GA-39 district approximately 26 years.
biography.notes: Not a prior federal officeholder. No voting record in Congress — scoring must rely on state legislative record and stated positions.

keyBillsAndActions.bill: SB 320 — Georgia Civil Rights Act of 2025
keyBillsAndActions.description: Would enact comprehensive state civil rights protections covering housing, public accommodations, and employment; prohibits discrimination on basis of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability, familial status, or national origin; also bans racial profiling and requires data collection on traffic stops
keyBillsAndActions.notes: Georgia currently one of only three states without comprehensive civil rights law

keyBillsAndActions.bill: SB 235 — HBCUs Innovation and Economic Prosperity Planning Districts Commission
keyBillsAndActions.description: Creates HBCUs Innovation and Economic Prosperity Planning Districts Commission under the University System of Georgia
keyBillsAndActions.status: Passed Georgia Senate 46-7, February 26 (session year not confirmed in search results, likely 2025)
keyBillsAndActions.notes: Bipartisan passage; signals public investment in higher education, specifically HBCUs

keyBillsAndActions.bill: SB 182 — Georgia Music Office and Music Ready Communities Act
keyBillsAndActions.description: Creates Georgia Music Office and Music Ready Communities program
keyBillsAndActions.status: Passed unanimously out of Senate Committee on Economic Development and Tourism, February 27, 2025
keyBillsAndActions.notes: Signals attention to creative economy; bipartisan committee support

keyBillsAndActions.bill: SB 55 — Disabilities workforce / federal minimum wage compliance
keyBillsAndActions.description: Aids those with disabilities in the workforce; brings Georgia into compliance with federal minimum wage laws for workers with disabilities
keyBillsAndActions.status: Passed (session year not confirmed in search results)
keyBillsAndActions.notes: Bipartisan bill; sponsors included both Democratic and Republican senators

keyBillsAndActions.bill: SB 185 — Ban on gender-affirming care for transgender prison inmates
keyBillsAndActions.action: Yes vote (broke with majority of Democratic caucus)
keyBillsAndActions.description: Bans all gender-affirming medical care for transgender people in state prisons
keyBillsAndActions.status: Passed Georgia Senate March 2025; signed by Governor Kemp
keyBillsAndActions.halpernQuote: Not one tax dollar in Georgia has ever been spent on sex change surgeries for inmates. This bill simply makes explicit what is already the practice in Georgia, and yet here we are debating this as if it were some looming crisis.
keyBillsAndActions.halpernFollowUp: My vote does not change my commitment to the LGBTQ+ community. I will fight for protections that ensure transgender people in Georgia can live their life safely and freely and will fight back against real attacks on LGBTQ+ rights.
keyBillsAndActions.notes: SIGNIFICANT CONFLICT: This vote conflicts with her sponsorship of SB 320 which includes gender identity anti-discrimination protections. She framed her vote as a fiscal/policy pragmatism argument, not ideological opposition to trans rights. Flag for scorer.

pressReleasesAndStatements.quote: I am heartbroken to learn about the tragic and entirely preventable death of Amber Thurman, who lost her life due to delayed emergency medical care under Georgia's abortion ban.
pressReleasesAndStatements.additionalQuote: A stark reminder of how dangerous this law is — putting our healthcare providers in direct conflict with the Hippocratic Oath they swore to uphold, all while they fear the risk of prosecution. The trust that people have in their doctors erodes, and the access to essential care becomes dangerously limited.
pressReleasesAndStatements.additionalQuote2: I am angry when I consider that in a state like Georgia — a place with so much to offer and a history of setting powerful examples for the rest of the country — this is what we are becoming known for. Amber Thurman didn't have to die. But the system made it easier for her to do so — and that is simply unacceptable.
pressReleasesAndStatements.notes: Explicit, strong opposition to Georgia's abortion ban. Amber Thurman died in 2022 after being denied emergency medical care (dilation and curettage) due to Georgia's abortion ban; death confirmed preventable by Georgia Maternal Mortality Review Committee.

pressReleasesAndStatements.quote: The Hyundai-LG battery facility represents the largest industrial project in our state's history, with 8,500 promised jobs and billions of dollars in investment.
pressReleasesAndStatements.additionalQuote: Partnership also requires accountability. If there were violations of the law, they must be addressed in a way that protects both Georgia's integrity and our economic future.

positionConflicts.conflict: Voted YES on SB 185 (ban on gender-affirming care for transgender prison inmates, March 2025) while simultaneously co-sponsoring SB 320 (Georgia Civil Rights Act of 2025, which includes gender identity protections). She framed her SB 185 vote as fiscal pragmatism ('not one tax dollar in Georgia has ever been spent on this') rather than ideological opposition, and said it did not change her commitment to the LGBTQ+ community.
sources: AJC reporting on SB 185 vote, March 2025
positionConflicts.scorerNote: Scorer should assess whether this represents a genuine ideological position or a pragmatic political vote. Her stated reasoning was cost-based (no new policy change, just codifying existing practice), but she broke with the majority of her Democratic caucus.

positionConflicts.conflict: Her response to the Hyundai ICE raid was carefully calibrated — she called for transparency and accountability rather than condemning the raid outright. She acknowledged 'if there were violations of the law, they must be addressed.' This is notably more moderate than a blanket anti-enforcement stance.
sources: Georgia Senate Press Office letter to Gov. Kemp, September 2025
positionConflicts.scorerNote: Insufficient evidence to place her strongly on immigration enforcement axis. Her concern was primarily economic/transparency-focused, not a civil liberties argument.

evidenceSummary.confidenceNotes: 4+ years of Georgia State Senate record provides moderate evidence base. Key limitation: she has never held federal office, so no congressional voting record exists. Many of her minority-party bills failed to pass (Republican supermajority in Georgia Senate), limiting signal from voting outcomes vs. bill sponsorship. Most evidence comes from advocacy statements, bill sponsorships, and press releases — these are strong directional signals but lower confidence than actual vote outcomes. The transgender prisoners vote is the most notable deviation from standard progressive positioning and must be surfaced for the scorer.
evidenceSummary.biasAlert: Halpern is running in a D+25 district vacated by a progressive incumbent (Lucy McBath). The competitive primary is against Chris Capparell (D). Her stated positions are broadly aligned with national Democratic mainstream, but she has demonstrated willingness to break with her caucus on at least one LGBTQ issue. Her background as a marketing executive and community arts leader differs from a typical progressive activist profile.
